transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose the main reason I finally made the appointment—which, honestly, took me weeks to actually do, because my schedule at the firm is just relentless right now, especially with the end of the quarter coming up and all the portfolio reviews—but anyway, I came in because I barely sleep in any useful way anymore. I mean, I get into bed, usually around 11:30 or midnight, after I’ve finally closed my laptop, but then I just lie there. My brain just won't shut off. I’ll be staring at the ceiling, replaying client models in my head, worrying about whether I factored in the right risk variables for the new tech acquisitions, going over every little spreadsheet cell. And even when I do finally drift off, it’s not real sleep. I’ll wake up at 3 or 4 in the morning, like clockwork, and my stomach will just be completely tight, tied in knots. And once I'm up at 4 AM, that’s it. I just lie there until my alarm goes off at 6. Then I have to get up, put on a suit, and go into the office feeling like I never actually rested at all. It’s been happening for so long now, and it’s just exhausting trying to function as an analyst when you’re running on fumes, you know?
Do you experience excessive worry or anxiety during the day, outside of when you're trying to sleep?

Not really, no. It's actually kind of strange, because you'd think with how my brain completely spins out of control at night, I'd be a nervous wreck at the office. But during the day... it's not really worry or anxiety. It's more just this endless, exhausting push to get things done when I have absolutely zero energy. 

Like, I'll be sitting at my desk—I have this office where the glass walls mean everyone can see in, so I always have to look sharp and on top of things—and I'm staring at my screens, looking at the Bloomberg terminal, checking the tech sector trends, and I'm not anxious at all. I'm just... running on empty. Completely drained. My junior analysts will come over to ask about a valuation model or a discrepancy in a report, and I just methodically go through it with them. I don't feel that tight knot in my stomach during the day like I do at 4 AM. I think I'm honestly just too deeply tired to be anxious when the sun is up. 

I just go from meeting to meeting, pouring over spreadsheets, drinking cup after cup of coffee that doesn't even do anything anymore, just trying to survive the day until 6 or 7 PM so I can finally commute back home. It's almost like my brain is too numb during the day to muster up the energy to worry. It's only later, when the house is quiet and I'm actually supposed to be resting, that the worrying actually kicks in and the thoughts start racing. So, no, during the workday, I wouldn't say I'm experiencing anxiety, I'm really just trying to keep my head above water because I'm so incredibly exhausted from the night before.
Do you ever experience sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've heard of people having panic attacks, where they feel like they're having a heart attack or they can't breathe, but I don't get anything like that. It's not a sudden spike of fear or anything intense. Like I said, it's more of a slow, grinding exhaustion during the day, and then at night, it's just that relentless, quiet worrying about work. But it never peaks into some sort of terrifying episode. 

Even when I'm looking at a really bad quarter for a client, or the market takes a sudden dive—like last week when the tech sector took a hit and my inbox was just flooding with panicked emails from portfolio managers—I don't feel intense fear. I just sit there at my desk, feeling completely weighed down by it all, and I just slowly, methodically start drafting the response memos. There's no sudden rush of adrenaline or terror. Honestly, I think my body is just too depleted to even mount a response like that. It takes a certain amount of energy to feel intense fear, doesn't it? And I just don't have it. I'm just flat. Just incredibly, deeply flat and tired all the time. So, no, I wouldn't say I have any sudden episodes of intense fear or anything like that. It's all just one long, gray blur of fatigue.
Do you have any difficulty concentrating during the day?

Yeah, I really do. It’s actually becoming a huge problem, and honestly, it’s one of the things that’s scaring me the most right now, because my entire career is built on my ability to focus and catch the small details. Like, I’ve been an analyst for over twenty years. I know these financial models inside and out. But lately... it’s like trying to think through molasses. 

Just the other day, I was working on this valuation model for a mid-cap logistics company—something I’ve done a hundred times, it should have been completely second nature to me. But I sat there staring at the spreadsheet, and I just kept losing the thread of what I was doing. I’d look at the revenue projections, and then my mind would just go blank. I’d have to go back and reread the same base assumptions over and over again. I’d highlight a cell, look away for a second to check an email, and completely forget why I highlighted it or what formula I was supposed to be adjusting. 

What used to take me maybe forty-five minutes is now taking me three or four hours, just because I keep drifting off or losing my place. And the worst part is, even after spending all that extra time on it, I don’t trust my own work anymore. I’ll be sitting in the conference room waiting to give a presentation to the portfolio managers, and I’m just quietly panicking, convinced that I’ve missed something incredibly obvious because I couldn’t hold the information in my head long enough to synthesize it properly. It’s just... it’s exhausting. I’m spending so much energy just trying to force my brain to process basic information, and it’s still not working right.
Do you have any trouble falling asleep at the beginning of the night, or is it more that you wake up in the middle of the night and can't go back to sleep?

Honestly, it’s... well, it’s really both. That’s actually the main reason I finally came in to see someone, because I just... I barely sleep in any useful way anymore. It’s completely broken. 

At the beginning of the night, I’ll get into bed—usually around 11 or so—and I am physically just bone-tired, like I was saying earlier. But the second the lights are out, I'll just lie there awake, staring at the ceiling, and my brain starts replaying all the client models I was working on that day. I’ll be agonizing over the spreadsheet cells, wondering if I used the right discount rate for that logistics company, or if I missed a regulatory risk in a tech portfolio. It just loops and loops. I'm just lying there for hours, completely exhausted but unable to turn the projector off in my head.

And then, if I finally do manage to drift off from sheer exhaustion, it never lasts. I’ll inevitably wake up at 3 or 4 in the morning. My eyes just snap open, and my stomach is completely tied in knots. It’s that tight, awful feeling in my gut I mentioned before. The room is pitch black, the house is dead silent, but my mind is already back at the office. I’ll look at the clock on my nightstand and see 3:17 AM, and I just know I’m not going back to sleep. I’ll toss and turn, try to adjust the pillows, maybe try to focus on my breathing, but it’s completely useless. 

So by the time my actual alarm goes off at 6 AM, I have to physically force myself out from under the covers, and I go to work feeling like I never actually rested at all. It’s like I just closed my eyes for a five-minute blink and spent the rest of the night running a marathon in my head. I’m just so profoundly depleted before I even step onto the train for my commute. It’s every single night now, just this endless, punishing cycle.
Has your lack of energy affected your social life or relationships outside of work?

Oh, God, yes. It’s affected everything. I mean, my whole life has just shrunk down to the bare minimum. It’s like I have this tiny, finite bucket of energy every day, and work just drains it dry before I even leave the building. And even then, I’m barely holding on at the office. I actually… I received a formal performance warning last month. My managing director pulled me into his office because my models have been sloppy, and my presentations just aren’t as sharp as they used to be. He told me I’m missing things, and that it’s starting to reflect poorly on the team. So I’m pouring every ounce of energy I have into just trying not to get fired, and there is absolutely nothing left for anything else. 

I used to have a life outside of the firm, I really did. I’ve been part of this book club with some friends from college for, I don’t know, almost fifteen years? We used to meet on the first Thursday of every month, have wine, actually talk about the books, catch up on each other’s lives. But I haven’t been since… maybe October? I just can’t do it. The thought of sitting in someone’s living room, trying to force myself to make conversation and pretend I care about the plot of a novel when I can barely keep my eyes open… it’s just impossible. I text them an excuse every time. I’ve run out of excuses, honestly. They probably think I’m just blowing them off. 

And it’s not just that. I used to volunteer on Saturday mornings, teaching financial literacy to high school kids in the city. I loved doing that. It felt important, you know? Like I was using my skills for something good. But I had to stop showing up for that, too. I’d wake up on Saturday morning, completely exhausted from not sleeping all week, and the idea of getting on the subway and standing in front of a classroom for two hours made me want to cry. So I just stopped going. I didn't even really give them a good reason. 

Even the small things, like my Tuesday night yoga class… I used to go religiously. It was my way to decompress. I haven't unrolled my mat in months. I just go home, order takeout because I’m too tired to cook, and sit on the couch staring at the wall until it’s time to go to bed and not sleep again. So, yeah, my social life is completely gone. I’m just… I’m not participating in my own life anymore. I’m just existing, and barely even managing that.
Is there something specific at work that you think is causing your sleep problems?

Well, I mean... I've asked myself that same question, honestly, a thousand times. Because you'd think, right? You'd think there must be some big, looming deadline right now, or a specific client blowing up my phone, or some massive deal on the verge of collapsing. But it's not... it's not actually anything current like that. 

The truth is, this... this whole situation, the not sleeping, the brain just spinning completely out of control in the middle of the night... it’s actually been going on for about three years now. Yeah, three years. It all really traces back to when the firm went through this massive merger that completely reorganized our Caribbean-market division. 

I was heavily involved in that sector at the time, and when the merger happened, it was just... I mean, it was absolute chaos. They brought in all this new leadership, they changed our entire reporting structure, and suddenly every single financial model I had built for our Caribbean assets over the previous decade was being torn apart and scrutinized by these new guys who didn't even understand the regional regulatory nuances. I was working these grueling, ridiculous hours just trying to defend my work and keep the division's transition on track, and that’s... that's when my sleep just broke. I’d go to bed terrified about what the new partners were going to demand the next morning, or if I'd miscalculated a currency risk. 

But the frustrating thing is... the reorganization eventually ended. The dust settled, the Caribbean division integrated, and the actual workload went back to a relatively normal pace. But my sleep never recovered. It’s like my brain flipped a panic switch three years ago during that merger and just... broke off the handle so I couldn't turn it back down. 

So, no, there’s no specific crisis happening right now that's causing it. It’s just been three solid years of this exact same exhaustion, every single night. Three years of lying awake, staring at the ceiling, all stemming from a corporate restructure that’s been over for ages. It's just... it's been three years, and I don't know how much longer my body can actually take it.
Do you think your sleep problems are related to your overall mental health or could they be caused by a physical issue?

I mean... I've wondered about that. You know, if maybe there's just something physically broken in my body that's keeping me awake. But... no, I really don't think it's a physical issue. I honestly think it all comes down to my mental state, because of how I feel during the day. It's not just that I'm tired from not sleeping. It's... it's so much more than that. 

Most days I move through the office, and honestly, even my own apartment, with this incredibly heavy, gray feeling. It's just this suffocating grayness that colors absolutely everything. It’s like I’m wearing one of those lead aprons they put on you at the dentist, just dragging this invisible weight around with me everywhere I go. I'm just... I'm just going through the motions of a life. I sit at my desk, I stare at my dual monitors, I click through the financial models, but I'm not really there. I'm just a ghost pretending to work. 

And my emotions are just so incredibly frayed, so close to the surface all the time. It's actually embarrassing. I'll be walking down the hall, or someone will stop by my door to ask me a completely normal, mundane question—like, "Hey, did you attach the updated revenue projections to that email?" or "Do you know if the printer on the fourth floor is working?"—and I will literally have to bite the inside of my cheek because I am trying so, so hard not to cry. Over a printer! Or a spreadsheet! I just stand there, forcing this stiff smile, nodding, while my throat closes up and my eyes start to burn, and I'm just praying they don't notice that I'm completely falling apart in front of them. 

And it doesn't stop when I leave work. I'll go home, and I'll just be standing in my kitchen, looking at the microwave, and that same heavy, gray feeling is right there with me. It never lifts. So, when you ask if it's mental... yes. It has to be. Because a physical problem wouldn't make me feel like I'm on the absolute verge of weeping every single second of the day, would it? It's just this constant, miserable emotional weight, and I spend so much energy just trying to hold back the tears and pretend I'm a functioning human being, that by the time night comes, my brain is just a mess. I really think the sleep is just a casualty of whatever this... this awful, heavy sadness is.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before your sleep problems started?

I mean, honestly, no. Not at all. It’s like... it’s like everything I used to enjoy has just been drained of all its color, you know? I mentioned my book club and the volunteering, and how I just stopped going because I'm too tired, but it's not even just the exhaustion keeping me away. Even if I somehow magically had the energy to get on the subway and go, I don't think I'd get any joy out of it anymore. 

Like, I used to love reading. I'd devour a novel in a weekend. I loved getting lost in a story, the feeling of connecting with characters, the whole experience of it. Now, if I even try to pick up a book—and I have tried, I really have, I have a stack of them on my nightstand just mocking me—I read the same paragraph over and over, and it's just words on a page. It means nothing to me. There's no spark, no interest, no... nothing. 

And it's the same with food. I used to really enjoy trying new restaurants in the city. A few years ago, before the merger and the sleep issues and this awful grayness set in, I kept a spreadsheet—because of course I did, I'm an analyst—of all the new bistros and cafes I wanted to try in different neighborhoods. I'd make a whole Saturday out of it, walking around, trying a new place, really tasting the food. Now? Food is just... fuel. And barely even that. I order the same bland Thai noodles or a turkey sandwich almost every night because I don't care what it tastes like. I don't enjoy it. I just eat it so I don't pass out at my desk the next day. 

Even music... I used to listen to jazz when I worked, or put on a playlist when I was cleaning the apartment. I'd actually feel the music, you know? It would lift my mood. Now, if I put music on, it just feels like noise. It's just irritating noise that I want to turn off. 

So, no. I don't enjoy anything anymore. Everything I used to love just feels flat and pointless now. It’s like the capacity to feel pleasure or interest has just been completely scooped out of me, and I don't know how to get it back. It's just... gone.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you once found pleasurable?

Well, yeah... I mean, exactly like I was just saying a second ago about the reading and the food. It’s exactly that. I've completely lost interest. 

I don't know if I didn't explain it well enough just now, but it's not only that I don't get pleasure out of things when I do them, it's that the actual drive—the interest in even *trying* to do them in the first place—is just completely wiped out. Like with those books I mentioned sitting on my nightstand. I used to be the kind of person who was always planning my next novel, always researching things, always having some little project or a weekend plan going on. 

And now... I look at my weekends, and there is just zero desire to fill that time with anything at all. People at the office will ask what I'm doing for the weekend, you know, just making polite small talk by the coffee machine, and I just freeze up because I have absolutely nothing to say. I don't want to do anything. I don't want to go anywhere. The thought of even trying to muster up the interest to look up a movie, or follow up with that book club I abandoned, or even just walk through the park... it just feels like trying to run a marathon in waist-deep mud. 

So yes, to answer your question, the interest itself is just completely gone. It’s like that entire part of my personality just packed up and left three years ago during that merger, and I'm just sitting here waiting for it to come back, but it never does. I just... I really don't care about any of the things that used to make me who I am, if that makes sense.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure in your daily activities most of the time?

I... I feel like maybe I'm not explaining myself properly, or maybe we're just going in circles a little bit here, because I feel like I just answered this when we were talking about the food and the books and my weekends. But, yes. Yes, absolutely. To be completely clear, pleasure is just... it’s not a word that applies to my life anymore, in any capacity. 

And it’s not just the big things, like going out or hobbies, it’s the tiny daily activities, too. Like, I used to have this whole morning ritual. I’d get up and make a really nice pour-over coffee. I even bought this expensive copper gooseneck kettle a few years ago, back when I actually cared about things like the exact temperature of the water and taking the time to let the coffee grounds bloom. I used to stand by the window in my kitchen, holding this warm mug, looking out at the street, and I’d feel... good. Just a quiet, simple pleasure before logging on or heading out to the subway. 

Now? I still make the coffee, mostly because I need the caffeine to literally keep my eyes open while I stare at those spreadsheets all day, but I don't even taste it. I could be drinking hot water with dirt in it for all I care. I stand at that exact same window, and I feel absolutely nothing. No warmth, no comfort, no tiny spark of 'oh, this is a nice morning.' It's just a completely mechanical process. Wake up. Shower. Put on work clothes. Drink the brown liquid. Go to work. Try not to cry in front of my coworkers. Come home. Stare at the microwave. 

There is zero pleasure in any of it. Not in the coffee, not in the feeling of a hot shower, not in getting a lucky seat on the train... it's all just this endless, flat, gray expanse. So, yes, if you're asking if I'm unable to experience pleasure in my daily routine... most of the time? No, all of the time. Every single day. I just... I don't feel anything good anymore.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure in your daily activities most of the time?

Wait... I'm sorry, did you... did you just ask me the exact same question again? I feel like I'm losing my mind here. I mean, I know I'm exhausted, and I know my brain isn't working the way it used to, but I could swear you literally just asked me that exact phrase, word for word, and I just gave you this whole long explanation about my morning coffee routine and the shower and staring at the microwave. 

Is there... is there some part of that I didn't explain right? Or are you looking for something specific that I'm just not getting? Because I really don't know what else to tell you. I don't have anything new to add to that. Like I said, I try to be thorough, because in my line of work as an analyst, details matter, right? You have to look at all the variables, you have to paint the whole picture. So I'm trying to give you all the details about how my life is just this endless, flat, gray slog, but if you're just going to ask me the exact same thing again... I just don't know what you want me to say. 

I'm trying my best to answer you, I really am, but it takes so much energy just to sit here and talk about all of this, and having to repeat myself is just... it's really frustrating. So, no. I don't have any pleasure. None. I really don't have anything else to say about it. I just don't.
Have you had to take any time off work due to your current state?

Time off? I... I haven't taken any official leave, if that's what you mean. I mean, I have sick days piled up, but I force myself to go in, even though it's... it's a disaster. I probably *should* take time off, to be honest, because I'm just barely holding on by my fingernails there. 

Actually, it's funny you ask about work, because things have gotten really bad recently. I've always prided myself on my accuracy. You know, as an analyst, if your models are off, everything is off. The whole projection crumbles. And for years, I was the person they came to when they needed something bulletproof. But lately... my concentration is just shot. I can't hold the numbers in my head. I'll be staring at a spreadsheet I built from scratch two years ago, and it looks like a foreign language. 

And it's not just a feeling I have, it's actually affecting my job. I had to sit down with my manager last month—which was humiliating, by the way, just absolutely mortifying—and they gave me a formal performance warning. A formal warning. After fifteen years at this firm. They said my models were slipping, that there were glaring errors in my presentations that the junior analysts were catching. The junior analysts! And I couldn't even defend myself, because they were right. I just sat there in that glass conference room, nodding, feeling like I was watching my whole career dissolve, and I didn't even have the energy to fight for it.

And it's not just work, either. It's everything else that used to make me a functioning adult. I used to do this volunteer teaching thing on Tuesday nights—financial literacy for high school kids, you know, helping them understand credit and basic budgeting. I loved it. I really did. But I haven't been in months. I just stopped showing up. I sent one email saying I was unwell, and then I just ghosted them. Same with my yoga studio. I used to go three mornings a week, and now I'm paying for a membership I haven't used since the spring. And that book club I mentioned earlier? I haven't read a single page of the last four books, and I finally just stopped logging onto the Zoom calls. 

It's like my entire life outside of just surviving the workday has completely collapsed. And even the workday is falling apart now. So, no, I haven't taken time off, but I'm definitely not functioning. I'm just... I'm just taking up space at my desk, waiting for them to finally fire me.
Do you often feel guilty or worthless about things that have happened in your life or your current situation?

Worthless... yeah. Yes, worthless is... it's honestly the perfect word for it. Guilt, too, but the worthlessness is just so heavy right now. Especially after what I was just telling you about work and that performance warning. I mean, I’m forty-eight years old, I have a degree that I worked incredibly hard to get, I’ve been doing this for a long time, and I just feel like... like a complete and utter fraud who has completely lost her edge. 

It’s like, any time my manager questions one of my projections now—which, you know, in investment analysis, pushback is normal, you’re supposed to defend your models, that’s just how the industry works, we stress-test everything—but now? If they even ask a simple, routine question about how I arrived at a certain number, I don't see it as a normal work conversation anymore. I immediately hear it as this glaring confirmation that I'm just not as sharp as I used to be. My brain just jumps straight to, 'See? They know. Everyone can see I'm failing.' 

And then I just spiral. I’ll sit there in the meeting, or at my desk staring at the email, and this wave of... of just intense shame washes over me. I feel so guilty that I’m dragging the team down, that those junior analysts are having to pick up my slack and double-check my math. I feel absolutely worthless because my entire identity, for so long, was tied up in being the smart one, the reliable one, the one who could build these beautiful, flawless financial models that the partners could take straight to the bank. 

Now, if someone just asks, 'Hey, did you account for this variable?' I just crumble inside. I feel completely exposed. I'll go home and I'll replay that one tiny, probably insignificant interaction in my head for hours, just beating myself up, telling myself how useless I am, how I don't deserve my salary, how it’s only a matter of time before everyone realizes I'm just completely incapable of doing my job anymore. It's exhausting, honestly. To constantly feel like you're letting everyone down and that you have absolutely no value left to offer. So, yes... I feel worthless constantly. It never really turns off.
Have you ever thought about death or wished you were dead?

Death? No. No, I haven't... I don't have thoughts like that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I am absolutely miserable, as I've been saying. Every single day just feels like I'm dragging this immense, invisible weight around, and sometimes I do just want the pressure to stop. The constant feeling of failing, the anxiety about the models at work, the guilt—I just want a break from it all. 

Sometimes I'll be lying in bed—because I spend a lot of time just lying there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about how I used to be able to handle a sixty-hour work week and still have the energy to function like a normal human being—and I'll just wish I could go to sleep and not have to wake up and do it all over again the next day. Like I just want to hit a pause button on the entire world. Just put everything on hold so I can sleep for a month, or a year, and not have to face that glass conference room or those junior analysts ever again. 

But actually wanting to die? Or wishing I was dead? No. No, I don't have that. It's more of a... a profound exhaustion with existing the way I am right now, if that makes sense. I don't want to end my life, I just want the life I'm currently living to not be so unbearably heavy and gray. Because, you know, my brain still works enough to look at things logically, and I know that checking out entirely isn't a solution. I just don't have those kinds of dark thoughts about ending it all. I just want to feel like myself again, or at least not feel like *this* anymore. So, no, I'm not thinking about death. I'm just... I'm just so tired of being here, like this.
Have you experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in most activities for at least two weeks?

Loss of interest? No, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. I mean, it’s not like I don’t care about things anymore. Like I mentioned earlier with the volunteer teaching... I still think about those kids all the time. I had this one student, a junior, who was finally starting to grasp the concept of compound interest after struggling with it for weeks, and I genuinely care about whether he's keeping up with his mock portfolio. I want to be there. I really, truly do. 

And the book club, too—I'm actually still buying the books! I have the last four sitting in a stack right on my nightstand. The newest one is this sprawling historical biography, which is usually exactly the kind of thing I love, and I keep looking at the cover every single night thinking, 'I really want to dive into that.' I even read the reviews online because I want to know what the group is discussing. So the desire is there. The interest is absolutely still there. 

It's not that I don't find pleasure in the idea of these things. If I could just snap my fingers and magically be in that classroom, or be on my yoga mat in the back row of the studio—I always used to take the back row near the window because the morning light comes in just perfectly—I know I would enjoy it. I know I would. It’s just that the bridge between wanting to do it and actually having the physical and mental energy to get dressed, leave the apartment, and interact with other human beings... that bridge is just completely burned right now. 

The exhaustion, and this heavy, suffocating dread about work that I carry around all day, it just swallows up all my capacity to act on those interests. It takes everything I have just to log onto my computer for my job, so by the time the evening rolls around, I have nothing left in the tank for the things I actually like. So, no, I haven't lost interest at all, if I'm being honest. I'm just... I'm just too depleted to actually participate in the things I still care about.
Have you experienced a depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Two weeks? Oh, it’s... it’s been so much longer than two weeks. I wish it had only been two weeks. But yes, absolutely. It’s almost every single day. Most days, I just move through the office, and even when I'm just at home in my apartment, I carry this incredibly heavy, gray feeling with me everywhere I go. It's like I'm walking around wrapped in a wet wool blanket. I'm just going through the motions of my life—making the coffee, pulling up the market data, answering emails—but there's no color to any of it anymore. It's all just this suffocating gray. 

And it makes everything feel so overwhelmingly precarious. I’ll be at my desk, or grabbing water in the breakroom, and someone will come up and ask me a completely normal, mundane question. Something like, 'Hey, did you get the updated Q3 figures?' or 'Are we still on for the 2 PM review?' And I swear to you, I have to use every single ounce of willpower I possess just to hold it together and try not to cry right there in front of them. Over a completely normal question! It’s humiliating. I’m a senior analyst, I’ve been in this firm for years, and I’m standing there biting the inside of my cheek so I don't burst into tears over a routine status update. 

But that heavy feeling is just always right there. It sits right at the back of my throat, all day long. It doesn't matter if I'm staring at a complex financial model at work or just sitting on my sofa in my apartment staring at the wall, the sadness doesn't lift. I used to tell myself, 'Oh, you're just stressed, just get through this reporting cycle and you'll feel better.' But the cycle ends, and the mood doesn't change. The grayness is just... it's just always there, from the moment I open my eyes until the day is finally over.
Have you experienced a significantly depressed mood or loss of interest in activities for at least two weeks?

Yes, exactly, like I was just trying to explain... it's really that depressed mood more than losing the actual interest in things. And it's been going on for so much longer than a couple of weeks. It's just as I described a moment ago. Most days I move through the office, and then I take the subway home and move through my apartment, just completely weighed down by this heavy, gray feeling. 

I'm really just... I'm just going through the motions of being a person at this point. I wake up, I make the coffee, I open the spreadsheets, I turn off the lights at night, but I'm not really *in* my life anymore, if that makes sense. I'm just watching myself do these things through this awful filter. 

And it's all so painfully close to the surface, you know? Like I mentioned about the breakroom earlier, I'm constantly just trying not to cry when someone asks me a normal question. It doesn't even have to be about work. Someone could ask me about the weather, or if I want in on a group lunch order from the deli downstairs, and I just feel my eyes well up and my chest tighten. doctor.question: Do you often feel guilty or worthless about things that have happened in your life or your current situation?

target_item.name: Low_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: When a manager questions one of my projections, I immediately hear it as confirmation that I'm not as sharp as I used to be and that everyone can see I'm failing.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about feeling worthless directly matches the symptom of low self-esteem, which involves a persistent tendency to evaluate oneself as incompetent or worthless.

patient.answer:
Worthless... yeah. Yes, worthless is... it's honestly the perfect word for it. Guilt, too, but the worthlessness is just so heavy right now. Especially after what I was just telling you about work and that performance warning. I mean, I’m forty-eight years old, I have a degree that I worked incredibly hard to get, I’ve been doing this for a long time, and I just feel like... like a complete and utter fraud who has completely lost her edge. 

It’s like, any time my manager questions one of my projections now—which, you know, in investment analysis, pushback is normal, you’re supposed to defend your models, that’s just how the industry works, we stress-test everything—but now? If they even ask a simple, routine question about how I arrived at a certain number, I don't see it as a normal work conversation anymore. I immediately hear it as this glaring confirmation that I'm just not as sharp as I used to be. My brain just jumps straight to, 'See? They know. Everyone can see I'm failing.' 

And then I just spiral. I’ll sit there in the meeting, or at my desk staring at the email, and this wave of... of just intense shame washes over me. I feel so guilty that I’m dragging the team down, that those junior analysts are having to pick up my slack and double-check my math. I feel absolutely worthless because my entire identity, for so long, was tied up in being the smart one, the reliable one, the one who could build these beautiful, flawless financial models that the partners could take straight to the bank. 

Now, if someone just asks, 'Hey, did you account for this variable?' I just crumble inside. I feel completely exposed. I'll go home and I'll replay that one tiny, probably insignificant interaction in my head for hours, just beating myself up, telling myself how useless I am, how I don't deserve my salary, how it’s only a matter of time before everyone realizes I'm just completely incapable of doing my job anymore. It's exhausting, honestly. To constantly feel like you're letting everyone down and that you have absolutely no value left to offer. So, yes... I feel worthless constantly. It never really turns off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had thoughts of death or suicidal ideation
doctor.question: Have you ever thought about death or wished you were dead?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Death? No. No, I haven't... I don't have thoughts like that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I am absolutely miserable, as I've been saying. Every single day just feels like I'm dragging this immense, invisible weight around, and sometimes I do just want the pressure to stop. The constant feeling of failing, the anxiety about the models at work, the guilt—I just want a break from it all. 

Sometimes I'll be lying in bed—because I spend a lot of time just lying there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about how I used to be able to handle a sixty-hour work week and still have the energy to function like a normal human being—and I'll just wish I could go to sleep and not have to wake up and do it all over again the next day. Like I just want to hit a pause button on the entire world. Just put everything on hold so I can sleep for a month, or a year, and not have to face that glass conference room or those junior analysts ever again. 

But actually wanting to die? Or wishing I was dead? No. No, I don't have that. It's more of a... a profound exhaustion with existing the way I am right now, if that makes sense. I don't want to end my life, I just want the life I'm currently living to not be so unbearably heavy and gray. Because, you know, my brain still works enough to look at things logically, and I know that checking out entirely isn't a solution. I just don't have those kinds of dark thoughts about ending it all. I just want to feel like myself again, or at least not feel like *this* anymore. So, no, I'm not thinking about death. I'm just... I'm just so tired of being here, like this.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is severe enough to be considered a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in most activities for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Loss of interest? No, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. I mean, it’s not like I don’t care about things anymore. Like I mentioned earlier with the volunteer teaching... I still think about those kids all the time. I had this one student, a junior, who was finally starting to grasp the concept of compound interest after struggling with it for weeks, and I genuinely care about whether he's keeping up with his mock portfolio. I want to be there. I really, truly do. 

And the book club, too—I'm actually still buying the books! I have the last four sitting in a stack right on my nightstand. The newest one is this sprawling historical biography, which is usually exactly the kind of thing I love, and I keep looking at the cover every single night thinking, 'I really want to dive into that.' I even read the reviews online because I want to know what the group is discussing. So the desire is there. The interest is absolutely still there. 

It's not that I don't find pleasure in the idea of these things. If I could just snap my fingers and magically be in that classroom, or be on my yoga mat in the back row of the studio—I always used to take the back row near the window because the morning light comes in just perfectly—I know I would enjoy it. I know I would. It’s just that the bridge between wanting to do it and actually having the physical and mental energy to get dressed, leave the apartment, and interact with other human beings... that bridge is just completely burned right now. 

The exhaustion, and this heavy, suffocating dread about work that I carry around all day, it just swallows up all my capacity to act on those interests. It takes everything I have just to log onto my computer for my job, so by the time the evening rolls around, I have nothing left in the tank for the things I actually like. So, no, I haven't lost interest at all, if I'm being honest. I'm just... I'm just too depleted to actually participate in the things I still care about.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I move through the office and even my apartment with this heavy, gray feeling, like I'm just going through the motions and trying not to cry when someone asks me a normal question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is specifically asking if I have experienced a depressed mood for most of the day, which directly corresponds to the Depressed_Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? Oh, it’s... it’s been so much longer than two weeks. I wish it had only been two weeks. But yes, absolutely. It’s almost every single day. Most days, I just move through the office, and even when I'm just at home in my apartment, I carry this incredibly heavy, gray feeling with me everywhere I go. It's like I'm walking around wrapped in a wet wool blanket. I'm just going through the motions of my life—making the coffee, pulling up the market data, answering emails—but there's no color to any of it anymore. It's all just this suffocating gray. 

And it makes everything feel so overwhelmingly precarious. I’ll be at my desk, or grabbing water in the breakroom, and someone will come up and ask me a completely normal, mundane question. Something like, 'Hey, did you get the updated Q3 figures?' or 'Are we still on for the 2 PM review?' And I swear to you, I have to use every single ounce of willpower I possess just to hold it together and try not to cry right there in front of them. Over a completely normal question! It’s humiliating. I’m a senior analyst, I’ve been in this firm for years, and I’m standing there biting the inside of my cheek so I don't burst into tears over a routine status update. 

But that heavy feeling is just always right there. It sits right at the back of my throat, all day long. It doesn't matter if I'm staring at a complex financial model at work or just sitting on my sofa in my apartment staring at the wall, the sadness doesn't lift. I used to tell myself, 'Oh, you're just stressed, just get through this reporting cycle and you'll feel better.' But the cycle ends, and the mood doesn't change. The grayness is just... it's just always there, from the moment I open my eyes until the day is finally over.

inference.note: Added F32.1 as the patient's symptoms of depressed mood, loss of interest, and worthlessness could indicate a major depressive disorder, in addition to F32.0 for depressive episode and F41.1 for anxiety which might still be underlying despite the patient's denial of anxiety during the day

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a significantly depressed mood or loss of interest in activities for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I move through the office and even my apartment with this heavy, gray feeling, like I'm just going through the motions and trying not to cry when someone asks me a normal question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of depressed mood or loss of interest. Depressed mood directly matches the symptom profile for S024.

patient.answer:
Yes, exactly, like I was just trying to explain... it's really that depressed mood more than losing the actual interest in things. And it's been going on for so much longer than a couple of weeks. It's just as I described a moment ago. Most days I move through the office, and then I take the subway home and move through my apartment, just completely weighed down by this heavy, gray feeling. 

I'm really just... I'm just going through the motions of being a person at this point. I wake up, I make the coffee, I open the spreadsheets, I turn off the lights at night, but I'm not really *in* my life anymore, if that makes sense. I'm just watching myself do these things through this awful filter. 

And it's all so painfully close to the surface, you know? Like I mentioned about the breakroom earlier, I'm constantly just trying not to cry when someone asks me a normal question. It doesn't even have to be about work. Someone could ask me about the weather, or if I want in on a group lunch order from the deli downstairs, and I just feel my eyes well up and my chest tighten. It’s exhausting to live like this, having to constantly police my own face and my own voice all day long just so my coworkers don't see how close I am to completely falling apart over absolutely nothing. So, yes, the mood is definitely there. It's everywhere.

inference.note: F41.1 was ruled out due to the patient's description of their symptoms, which align more closely with depressive disorders than anxiety disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistently depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks, with significant impairment in social and occupational functioning. The patient reports feeling worthless, guilty, and having no pleasure in activities, which aligns with the diagnostic criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The absence of manic or hypomanic episodes and the presence of a depressed mood as the predominant symptom support the diagnosis of F32.0 (Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode) over other candidates.
